title: Planning Instruction with the Willingham Simple Memory Model: A Lesson on World Regions
author: SoL in the Wild
summary: This teacher-written post uses Daniel Willingham's Simple Memory Model as a lesson-planning checklist and shows it applied to a World Studies lesson on physical, cultural and economic regions. The author walks through each stage of the model (environment, attention, working memory, learning, long-term memory, remembering, forgetting) and for each one gives a planning question and the concrete routine used. Examples include choral response, SLANT, chunking the three region types, student-created fictional regions on mini whiteboards, mind maps, Leitner flashcards, emoji retrieval and interleaved questions in later units. The central claim is that learning is not exposure, and that instruction succeeds to the degree that it respects how memory works. Sweller's line that instruction without knowledge of cognitive architecture is blind frames the piece. It is a practical model-to-classroom translation, though it reports one lesson rather than evidence of outcomes.
points: The model works as a planning checklist because each stage prompts a design question, from what students will attend to through how forgetting will be reduced.
Chunking the content into three region types, each with an example and a short check, is offered as a concrete way to manage working memory load.
Encoding is deepened by having students generate and label their own fictional examples and build a scaffolded mind map.
Spaced retrieval through Leitner flashcards and interleaved questions in later units is the mechanism meant to keep the concepts fluent weeks later.
quotes: One of the central findings from cognitive science is that learning is inseparable from memory. If nothing has been retained in long-term memory, then no learning has occurred.

When I plan lessons, I now use the model as a kind of cognitive checklist. It forces me to ask: What will students actually attend to? How do I prevent working memory overload? How will I promote durable encoding, retrieval, and resistance to forgetting?
This structured environment reduces cognitive interference from unnecessary items and keeps attention directed towards instruction.
Cognitive science shows that explaining to others is a powerful form of rehearsal: it requires retrieval, comparison, and organization, all of which strengthen memory traces.

In addition, students create flashcards for the key terms (region, physical region, cultural region, economic region) with definitions and examples. These cards feed into the Leitner flashcard system, ensuring that their schema is not only built but also reinforced through spaced retrieval.

It reminds me that learning is not equivalent to exposure. Students do not learn because material was “covered” in class. They learn because information passed through working memory, was encoded into long-term memory, and was later retrieved and reinforced.

For me as a teacher, the model is both a warning and a guide. The warning is that without attention, encoding, and retrieval, content will be forgotten, regardless of how engaging my lesson feels. The guide is that if I deliberately design instruction to align with each stage of the model, I dramatically increase the likelihood that students will not just understand content temporarily but retain it, retrieve it, and use it to build further knowledge.
